about: What the shipped editions actually cost and actually hold, measured by driving each published artifact in headless Chromium on 2026-09-11. Two questions are answered here and nothing else: how an edition scales with its record count (page bytes, load time, JS heap), and how much lodging stock its record layer already carries. Load time and heap are single-run figures from one container under one browser build - they establish an order of magnitude and a slope, not a benchmark suite, and the `method` field says so. The lodging counts are exact: a count of records whose own `kind` field names a lodging use, not a heuristic over free text.

method.source: the published artifact for each edition, fetched and title-verified the same day (docs/PUBLISH_MAP.md)
method.load_ms: wall time from navigation start until window.BA.listings is a non-empty array; one run per edition, single container, no warm cache
method.heap_mb: performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize immediately after the record store is ready
method.lodging: count of listings whose `kind` field matches hotel|motel|inn|lodge|resort|hospitality. An earlier pass that also matched the `src` field over-counted uscorridor by more than tenfold (31,117 against 2,955) and was discarded - source strings are not use classes.
method.not_measured: interaction latency under a real pointer, mobile-device memory ceilings, and time-to-interactive as a user would perceive it. Those need a device lab, not a container.

kinds: Inn, lodge, rooming or fraternity house — Room/dorm

findings.ceiling: JS heap, not page weight. The largest shipped edition already holds 1.02 GB of heap at 354,260 records; page bytes at the same point are only 16 MB. Adding records costs roughly 54 bytes on the wire and 3 KB in memory, so memory runs out about fifty times sooner than bandwidth does.
findings.load_is_not_linear_in_this_sample: 87,578 records loaded slower than 125,803 (19.8 s against 16.7 s), so single-run load time carries at least a few seconds of noise. The heap figures are monotonic in record count and are the ones to plan against.
